stories.headline: Superlatives for this MLB free agent class, from Lowe to Gausman
stories.summary: Next best move for Mets? Best free agency timing? We have a yearbook's worth of awards for the top MLB free agents.
stories.body:
We still have a week left of potential chaos before the expected lockout freezes all moves, so while we still have time, let's dig in to the MLB offseason with our annual free agent superlatives.

Not included: Tarik Skubal, the most superlative in this class. He's headed to the New York Mets, who will pay him, Juan Soto and Bo Bichette about the same as what the Milwaukee Brewers paid for their entire World Series-winning roster in 2026.

Best bet on a 32-year-old outfielder: Seiya Suzuki

In a weak year for position players, the top two are similar-looking outfielders: Suzuki and Randy Arozarena. Both will be entering their age-32 seasons, are coming off their best seasons (5.1 WAR for Suzuki, 5.7 for Arozarena), hit right-handed, received qualifying offers and are projected to receive four-year, $90 million contracts.

Among the teams possibly looking for a corner outfielder: the Philadelphia Phillies (25th in OPS from their corner outfielders), Baltimore Orioles (26th), Toronto Blue Jays (27th), Houston Astros (30th) and San Diego Padres (17th, but they would move Fernando Tatis Jr. to second base). The Seattle Mariners might look to replace Arozarena with Suzuki. Which one would you rather have?

First off, given their age, both are risky bets -- or, at the minimum, unlikely to repeat those 5-WAR seasons. Check out the number of position players 32 or older who had 4-or-more WAR in recent seasons (with outfielders or DHs in parenthesis):

2026: 5 (Mike Trout)

2025: 9 (Aaron Judge, George Springer, Kyle Schwarber)

2024: 4 (Judge, Marcell Ozuna)

2023: 2

2022: 5 (Springer)

As you can see, not many players are remaining at an All-Star level in their 30s -- and this list includes only two players who played 100 games in the outfield (Judge and Trout). Still, with so many teams desperate for outfield help, both will get paid.

Why Suzuki over Arozarena? Suzuki has a couple of advantages. First, plate discipline. Suzuki ranked in the 89th percentile in chase rate and 91st percentile in walk rate; Arozarena comes in at the 42nd percentile in chase rate and 63rd percentile in walk rate (although he was hit by 26 pitches to boost his OBP). Suzuki also has better bat speed. The second big one is defense. Suzuki had excellent metrics in 2026, and Arozarena has been consistently below average in recent seasons. Suzuki has also been consistent: He's one of six players with 20-plus home runs and an .800 OPS in each of the past four seasons. Arozarena is the better baserunner (even though Suzuki is faster) and has been extremely durable (averaging 154 games played the past five seasons), but Suzuki's bat is more likely to play over the next four years.

Best second baseman if the price is right: Jazz Chisholm Jr.

Nineteen teams finished with an OPS below .700 from their second basemen -- eight of them below .675 -- so there are teams that need help at the position. Chisholm, Brandon Lowe and Luis Arraez are on the market (and Ketel Marte is available via trade). Lowe, coming off back-to-back 30-homer seasons and improved defense, is the top guy, but here are ESPN's projected contracts:

Lowe (5.3 WAR, 32 years old): Four years, $80 million

Arraez (2.9 WAR, 30 years old): Three years, $54 million

Chisholm (1.7 WAR, 29 years old): Two years, $46 million

If Lowe repeats his 2026 numbers and the defense is for real, he'll make the biggest impact the next couple of seasons. But we're back to age here, too. Paying Lowe from his age-32 to age-35 seasons for what he did at 30 and 31 is the risk. Only six second basemen have hit 30 home runs in a season at 32 or older. The last to do it was Robinson Cano in 2016; Jay Bell, Bret Boone (twice) and Jeff Kent (twice) did it between 1999 and 2003 when everyone was hitting home runs; and then you have to go all the way back to Joe Gordon in 1948 and Rogers Hornsby in 1929.

Arraez is a three-time batting champ who hit .310 in 2026 and almost never strikes out, so he presents a nice change of pace with his contact ability, but his OBP isn't great and he doesn't provide much power. Statcast metrics suddenly loved his defense at second base, which will help him receive a better contract than the one-year, $12 million deal he had with the San Francisco Giants for 2026.

But he lacks Chisholm's power/speed/defense upside -- although, admittedly, Chisholm rarely does all three of those things at his best in the same season. He's the youngest and most athletic of the trio, and he had 4.1 WAR in 2025 and 2.9 in 2024, when he hit .250/.328/.456 while averaging 28 home runs and 36 stolen bases. He also has positional flexibility, able to slide to third base or center field. On a short-term deal, Chisholm could be a big addition.

Best fit for Chicago White Sox: Clay Holmes

The White Sox must have had some plan in place when they dumped Luis Castillo's contract on the Colorado Rockies. They included Davis Martin to make the trade work, so the idea had to be that they could sign a pitcher better than Martin. But, in a matter of a few hours Tuesday, Trevor Rogers and then Freddy Peralta and then Kaima Taira agreed to deals, leaving Michael King as the only remaining starter in the top 10 from our free agent ranking -- and he's widely expected to return to San Diego. How about trying to steal Holmes away from the Cubs? He has a 3.44 ERA in his two years as a starter and is a groundball machine who keeps home runs in check (he missed time this past season, but that was due to fractured right fibula after getting hit by a comebacker).

Player needed to get the Phillies over the top: Brandon Lowe

Ahh, we just pumped up Chisholm, but the Phillies are worried only about the immediate future -- so, for them, betting on Lowe and his power is the way to go. In this piece last year, we had Alex Bregman to the Phillies; he went on to sign with the Chicago Cubs. The Phillies should have listened to us. Yes, signing Lowe would create a bit of an infield logjam, but Bryson Stott can shift to third (as he did after the Phillies traded for Arraez). It does leave the lineup lefty heavy, but imagine the home run damage Lowe might do at Citizens Bank Park -- and Lowe is less risky (and a better defender) than Teruaki Sato, the slugger from Japan who had been linked to the Phillies before he landed with ... the Cubs.

The reliever everyone wants: Adrian Morejon

Morejon has been outstanding the past three seasons with the Padres, with a 2.58 ERA in 233⅓ innings and while flashing a dominant four-pitch profile with durability. Over those three seasons, he's third in FanGraphs WAR among relievers while leading all relievers in innings. Everyone saw what the Brewers did in the postseason with a trio of left-handed relievers, so their title run probably helped Morejon's free agency.

ESPN forecasted a four-year, $88 million contract, which would be a huge average salary for a reliever who has never been a closer. It would be the third-highest total value for a reliever, behind Edwin Diaz's $102 million deal with the Mets (which he later opted out of to sign with the Dodgers) and Josh Hader's $95 million deal with the Astros.

Now for the "but ..." part of this. Relievers are volatile, even good ones. Check out how the highest-paid relievers in 2026 fared:

Hader ($19M): 1.01 ERA, 26 saves

Diaz ($17M): 8.68 ERA, seven saves

Devin Williams ($16M): 4.43 ERA, 16 saves

Tanner Scott ($16M): 2.69 ERA, 25 saves

Raisel Iglesias ($16M): 2.55 ERA, 34 saves

Ryan Helsley ($14M): 4.11 ERA, 8 saves

Scott and Iglesias were the only two to stay healthy, and only three of the six were effective. The next group making between $12 million and $14 million included Robert Suarez (effective but injured), Pete Fairbanks (6.31 ERA), Blake Treinen (29 innings) and Jeff Hoffman (lost closer role, traded). Only Aroldis Chapman was effective and healthy from this group. That's 11 relievers making at least $12 million, and only four who earned their salary. Still want Morejon at $20-plus million per season?

The next best move for the Mets: Kevin Gausman

A quick glance at Gausman's 4.51 ERA might suggest he's in decline as he enters his age-36 season, but the peripheral numbers remain above average (184 strikeouts against 47 walks) and the stuff hasn't deteriorated much -- his fastball still averaged 93.8 mph and his splitter and slider still generated swing-and-miss rates above 36%. Most importantly, check out his innings since 2021: 192, 174, 181, 193, 177. That's 31-plus starts every season, the rare pitcher who posts all six months, every year. He did serve up 26 home runs this past year, so he's a better fit for a more pitcher-friendly park -- a return to Toronto, San Diego ... or Citi Field, where Gausman would slide in nicely behind Skubal and Nolan McLean.

Player most likely to help the Brewers repeat: Casey Mize

Milwaukee isn't going to change the way it operates -- it let Jake Bauers leave for the Boston Red Sox on an affordable four-year, $58 million contract. The Brewers simply aren't going to commit long-term money to a player in his 30s, no matter what he meant to their success (even Christian Yelich's deal expires after 2028, which will create even more payroll flexibility).

The Brewers might want a starting pitcher, though. They have depth they can dip into, but the only starters worth more than 1.3 WAR this past season were Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson, so the Brewers are going to be careful with those young arms after the postseason run. Kyle Harrison was terrible in the second half, and Shane Drohan had significant injury issues in the minors in 2024 and 2025. Quinn Priester missed all of 2026.

Of course, the Brewers aren't going to spend big money on a free agent, which is why Mize could be the perfect fit. He's not exactly a reclamation project because he had a 2.70 ERA in 16 starts with the Detroit Tigers, but he fell apart after he was traded to the Padres (7.46 ERA in 10 starts). If any team can figure out what went wrong, it will be the Brewers -- and they could probably sign him on a relatively low-cost one-year deal. Mize is an extreme flyball pitcher, so their superb outfield defense will be a big help, and they could more comfortably go with a six-man rotation, especially early in the season.

Best free agent timing award: Ty France

An All-Star with the Mariners in 2022, France hit .247 over the next three seasons, producing just 1.3 WAR. At 31 years old, his career was in jeopardy, and he had to settle for a minor league contract with the Padres in 2026 just as spring training was kicking off. He made the team, worked his way into the starting lineup and was the Padres' best hitter, finishing with a .295/.363/.502 slash line and ranking 11th in the majors in wRC+ among hitters with 500 plate appearances.

Will teams buy in to the swing changes France made or view 2026 as a fluke season? The lack of offense available will help drive interest in him, plus he's a good defender at first base, so he should end up with a multiyear deal -- and the biggest payday of his career.

Player who will inevitably end up in Seattle: Alec Bohm

Every year, president of baseball operations Jerry Dipoto signs a veteran free agent hitter. It never works out, but one of these years, the Mariners will have to luck into the right move to fortify their offensive depth. Dipoto already acquired Maikel Garcia to play third base, so all Bohm has to do is DH, preferably just against left-handed pitchers, because that's what he's good at, hitting .302/.351/.503 in his career against southpaws.

stories.headline: Raheem Sterling avoids jail for dangerous driving
stories.summary: Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has avoided jail after admitting dangerously driving his Lamborghini while inhaling from a balloon on a motorway during rush hour before crashing into a metal gate.
stories.body:
Former England footballer Raheem Sterling has avoided jail after admitting dangerously driving his Lamborghini while inhaling from a balloon on a motorway during rush hour before crashing into a metal gate.

The 31-year-old gave no reaction as he was sentenced to 12 months imprisonment, suspended for 18 months, at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court for dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide on May 28.

He was also ordered to complete 100 hours unpaid work and was banned from driving for 24 months.

A driver who called police said he was "shocked" by what he saw, and another said she had "genuine concerns the driver might kill someone," a court previously heard.

Police bodyworn footage of Sterling's arrest at 9.15 a.m. shows him in the crashed car with two canisters on his lap as the officer tells him: "You can put that down mate."

Sterling pleaded guilty in September to driving a Lamborghini Urus dangerously on the M25, the M3, the A327 and Minley Road in Surrey.

He also admitted possession of six nitrous oxide canisters for wrongful inhalation, a class C drug, and failing to provide a specimen.

During the September hearing at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court, prosecutor Simon Jones said a number of calls were made between 7.45 a.m. and 8.52 a.m. about a black sports car and the manner it was being driven.

Witness Christopher Jennings called 999 at 7.49 a.m. after driving alongside Sterling's car on the M25, and "he was shocked by what he saw", Mr Jones said, and made clear "he sighted the defendant inhaling from the balloon".

Fiona Jennings -- driving on the southbound M3 at around 8.45 a.m. -- said she saw a black Lamborghini and described the driving as "absolutely horrendous" and "swerving in and out of lanes," the court heard.

"She had genuine concerns the driver might kill someone," Mr Jones told the court.

"She looked across, initially thought an air bag was in play, then realised in fact it was a large white inflated balloon and the neck of balloon was in mouth of the driver."

Dashcam footage released by the Crown Prosecution Service shows a black Lamborghini switching lanes multiple times before hitting a concrete barrier on the right side and continuing on the road.

Sterling had come off at junction 4a of the M3 before doing a loop on the A327 and, just after a roundabout, he came off the road.

The vehicle veered off the carriageway and "must have collided with either the sign or metal gate", which caused "substantial" damage to his car and all four wheels which prevented him from driving further, the court heard.

Sterling was taken to Basingstoke police investigation centre by officers and disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide," Mr Jones said.

He complied with an impairment test, but for a blood sample, Sterling asked to obtain legal advice before making a decision, Mr Jones added.

In the police sergeant's view "he was deliberately failing to provide a clear answer."

Sterling was later interviewed by police with legal representation present where he accepted he had been the driver and provided no comment answers about the driving.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said there was no dispute that this was a "top category case" because of prolonged driving and "at times" serious impairment which would have been short periods within the driving.

But the defence did not accept the damage to the car was serious and said there was "confusion" over the failure to provide a specimen.

Sterling scored 20 goals in 82 appearances for England, helping Gareth Southgate's side reach the 2018 World Cup semifinals and the final of Euro 2020.

He came through the academy at QPR before joining Liverpool, where he made his senior debut.

Sterling, who was born in Kingston, Jamaica, moved to Manchester City in 2015 and won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and the FA Cup in 2019.

He left for Chelsea in 2022 but after falling out of favour spent the 2024-25 season on loan at Arsenal.

After leaving Stamford Bridge, Sterling joined Dutch club Feyenoord on a short-term deal until the end of the season.

He is currently without a club.

Sterling was made an MBE in the 2021 Queen's Birthday Honours for services to racial equality in sport after fronting anti-racism and discrimination campaigns and speaking out against racism on and off the pitch for several years.

It came amid controversy over England fans booing players taking the knee at matches as a gesture against intolerance.

stories.headline: Fantasy football matchup ranks: Tyler Shough, Ashton Jeanty with prime matchups
stories.summary: The most and least favorable matchups in the NFL for this week's games at the four key fantasy positions.
stories.body:
Thanksgiving night brings us one of the most significant rivalries among interdivision teams: The Buffalo Bills and Kansas City Chiefs.

The Bills and Chiefs have met 10 times since the beginning of 2020, during which time Josh Allen and Patrick Mahomes have started the near entirety of their teams' games. Strangely enough, the Bills have won five of the teams' six regular-season matchups while the Chiefs have emerged victorious in all four of the team's postseason meetings.

It's a particularly intriguing matchup when considering the Bills' dramatic defensive turnaround. One of the eight most favorable matchups for an opposing quarterback, running back or tight end during the first six weeks of the season, directly preceding their Week 7 bye, the Bills have since transformed into one of the eight toughest matchups for an opponent at all four skill positions.

The Bills' bye-week adjustments, which they attribute to better communication and focus on third and fourth downs, have had a lot to do with it. It's such changes that demonstrate why the weekly Matchup Rankings account for only recent performance -- the past five weeks -- rather than the whole season. We want the most recent snapshot of a defense, to make the most informed lineup decisions.

For those panicking over what this means for Mahomes, Travis Kelce, Rashee Rice and potentially Kenneth Walker III (if healthy enough to play), however, there's a caveat to the Bills' recent defensive prowess: During their hot spell, they've faced a good share of backup quarterbacks, two of which entered for in-game injuries. Always consider the context, which is why while those four players got downgrades in my rankings for Week 12, none grades as a "must-sit."

To give you a head start on optimizing your matchups, what follows are the Week 12 Matchup Rankings. For those curious about the methodology behind the numbers, select here for a handy primer.

Quarterbacks

Matchups highlight: Tyler Shough, New Orleans Saints (at Cincinnati Bengals). He might be difficult to trust after he scored a mediocre 14.28 fantasy points in a similarly favorable Week 11 matchup, but there aren't many better matchup-driven quarterback choices than Shough on the Week 12 schedule. He has had a pattern of slow starts but strong finishes within games, as he has scored 61% of his fantasy points for the season after halftime, and 38% while trailing on the scoreboard after halftime. That adheres well to this matchup, against a Bengals team that has struggled against lower-tier quarterbacks for much of the year, and one that is favored by 10 points in a game with a 50.5 over/under.

Others to like:

Trevor Lawrence, Jacksonville Jaguars (versus Tennessee Titans)
Joe Milton, Philadelphia Eagles (at Dallas Cowboys, Thanksgiving Day, 4:30 p.m. ET)

Matchup to avoid: Bryce Young, Carolina Panthers (at Tampa Bay Buccaneers, "Monday Night Football"). After a strong start to the season, Young has fallen into a significant funk, averaging 12.04 fantasy points per game over the past five weeks. Among those games was a Week 7 home game against these Buccaneers, during which he scored 5.42 fantasy points, was sacked five times, intercepted twice and lost a fumble. Jared Goff's 20.36-point Week 11 outburst was the outlier when facing this matchup; the Buccaneers held higher-tier quarterbacks Joe Burrow, Jordan Love, Dak Prescott and Caleb Williams beneath 15 points.

Running backs

Matchups highlight: Ashton Jeanty, Las Vegas Raiders (at Cleveland Browns, "Sunday Night Football"). Note to the Raiders: Feature Jeanty once again. Please. Jeanty broke off a pair of 40-plus-yard plays, both of which had him clocked at faster than 20 mph per NFL Next Gen Stats, in Week 12, demonstrating his big-play potential. He should play a significant role in the Raiders' Sunday night matchup with the Browns, who struggled mightily to defend running backs in the four weeks leading up to their Week 11 bye. During that time, the Browns' 0.86 fantasy points per rushing attempt afforded to the position was the league's most.

Others to like:

Cam Skattebo, New York Giants (at Indianapolis Colts)
Bhayshul Tuten, Jaguars (versus Titans)
Ollie Gordon II, Miami Dolphins (versus New York Jets)

Matchup to avoid: Jonathan Taylor, Colts (versus Giants). The Colts' quarterback issues and rebuilding status has severely hampered his fantasy production. Taylor has averaged 8.8 fantasy points over his past four games, a rate exceeded by 31 other running backs during that time, as well as one that's less than half the 19.6 he averaged over the season's first seven weeks. The opposing Giants, meanwhile, haven't allowed a running back to reach the 10-point threshold in fantasy since Week 6, and for the season, they've held the position to the ninth-fewest points per carry (0.54).

Wide receivers

Matchups highlight: Jakobi Meyers, Jaguars (versus Titans). Parker Washington might be the Jaguars wide receiver you'd prefer to have, but Meyers also warrants a look for Week 12. Meyers has seen at least an 18% target share, as well as at least one red-zone target, in each of his past five games, during which time six of the latter came in the end zone. That's the kind of usage you want to see ahead of a matchup with the league's worst defense for the season against wide receivers (+10.6 Adj. FPA). The Titans have seen two different wide receivers exceed 15 fantasy points in each of their past three games, and while the Jaguars' second player to do so in Week 10 was Josh Cameron, Meyers seems likely to be the matchup benefactor in the rematch.

Others to like:

Chris Olave, Saints (at Bengals)
Ladd McConkey, Los Angeles Chargers (versus New England Patriots)
DeVonta Smith, Eagles (at Cowboys)
KC Concepcion, Browns (versus Raiders)

Matchup to avoid: Drake London, Atlanta Falcons (at Minnesota Vikings). He has fallen prey to his matchups -- he scored only 1.8 fantasy points in his worst one to date, against the Buccaneers in Week 8 -- and bad backup quarterback play -- he scored 14.4 points combined while working with Cooper Rush in Weeks 1-2 -- making this matchup particularly concerning. The Vikings might've afforded 22.9 fantasy points to Mike Evans in a surprise stinker defensively last week, but even including that game, they have the second-fewest Adj. FPA for the season (minus-5.8).

Tight ends

Matchups highlight: Chig Okonkwo, Washington Commanders (at Arizona Cardinals). He's one of the better positional values for Week 12, having scored 10-plus fantasy points in four of his past six games with a 20% target share during that time. The opposing Cardinals have struggled mightily to defend tight ends of late, most recently surrendering 25.4 fantasy points to Kelce in his most productive game in three years. In the two games before that, Tyler Higbee and Davis Allen combined for 19.6 points in Week 10 and AJ Barner scored 15.0 in Week 9 against the Cardinals.

Matchup to avoid: George Kittle, San Francisco 49ers (versus Seattle Seahawks). He's a tough player to sit, but this couldn't be a much worse matchup for the game's No. 4 tight end in fantasy points. The Seahawks limited Kittle to 7.4 fantasy points on six targets in their Week 5 matchup, and they held Kelce, Colston Loveland, Trey McBride and Brock Bowers to a combined 36.1 fantasy points on 20 targets in the past five weeks alone. For the season, the Seahawks are the No. 1 defense in terms of Adj. FPA (minus-5.2).

Matchup Rankings methodology

All 32 opposing defenses are broken out by position, with points-allowed data over the past five weeks of the NFL season calibrated to account for the difficulty of the schedule it faced. "Adj. FPA," or Adjusted Fantasy Points Allowed, shows how much more or less than players' weekly fantasy point averages that defense has held its collective opponents at that position. A positive number designates a favorable matchup; a negative number means that it is unfavorable.

stories.headline: Fantasy basketball: How to take advantage of the 76ers' rotations
stories.summary: Andre Snellings looks at how the 76ers are handling rotations, resting players and dishing out minutes, and explains how to take advantage of it.
stories.body:
Through Monday, Nov. 23, the Philadelphia 76ers have played 17 games, and their starting lineup has broken down to four general epochs.

They have had their entire starting five in six games; missed four games each from Joel Embiid and LeBron James and missed three games from Jaylen Brown. Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe have both missed only one game each.

While the stats from handful of games in any given epoch isn't enough to make definitive statements, we can start to see some tendencies. On the fantasy and player prop front, this leads us to revive The 76ers' Player Availability Flowchart.

The players on the team perform differently, based upon which of their teammates are available in a given game.

We know each player's season averages, so let's break down how their production trends and expected values have tended to change based on the absences of their star teammates.

Statistical trends
When Embiid is out

Maxey has increased his scoring average to 29.0 PPG (average 25.9 PPG) on similar field goal percentage (48.8 FG% vs. 49.5 FG%).
LeBron has scored more (18.7 PPG vs 16.1 PPG) and much more efficiently (58.3 FG% vs. 46.5 FG%) but his rebounds have been down (5.0 RPG vs. 6.8 RPG).
Both Brown (20.8 PPG, 46.3 FG% vs. 22.6 PPG, 49.4%) and Edgecombe (11.0 PPG, 40.0 FG% vs. 13.8 PPG, 46.2 FG%) have scored less on lower efficiency.

When LeBron is out

Embiid's production trends have been similar to LeBron's without Embiid: Embiid's scoring has gone up (28.3 PPG vs. 20.4 season average) on better efficiency (47.5 FG% vs 40.0 FG%) but his rebounds have decreased (6.7 RPG vs 8.9 RPG).
Maxey's production trend is also similar, with more points (28.8 PPG) but on better efficiency as well (52.9 FG%).
Brown and Edgecombe have both produced around their season averages in points (23.0 PPG for Brown, 14.0 PPG for Edgecombe) but on lower efficiency (47.1 FG% for Brown, 41.7 FG% for Edgecombe).

When Brown is out

LeBron has increased his scoring (21.0 PPG) and scoring efficiency (55.6 FG%).
Embiid's assists have gone way up (7.7 APG), but his scoring efficiency has dropped precipitously (36.2 FG%) on similar volume (20.7 PPG).
Edgecombe's scoring volume (17.7 PPG) and efficiency (51.4 FG%) have both increased.
Maxey only played in two of the three games Brown sat, but he struggled with lower scoring volume (22.0 PPG) and efficiency (46.7 FG%), and also dished fewer assists (4.0 APG).

What the trends tell us
When either Embiid or LeBron have sat, Maxey and the one who played have both increased their scoring volume and scoring efficiency. This tracks, as these are the three best team-offense creators on the team. All three are very comfortable with the ball in their hands, making decisions to generate shots for either themselves or their teammates.

When all are available to play, they each have to play more off the ball than any are used to in their careers. But when one or more of the trio sits, the other(s) get to handle the ball and create their own shot more, which is in their comfort zones. Maxey has only sat out one game this season, but in that game Embiid dropped 26 points and LeBron 22...following a similar trend.

In fact, LeBron increased his scoring and efficiency when any of the other starters sat. Including the one game that Edgecombe sat, where LeBron dropped 18 points on 53% from the field. As expected when he joined such a strong lineup, it's clear that LeBron is sacrificing his stats on a per-game basis but can ramp up when called upon.

Interestingly, Brown's and Edgecombe's scoring efficiencies plummet and their volume dips as well when either LeBron or Embiid sit. Unlike LeBron, Brown and Edgecombe are largely iso players and/or finishers. When defenses don't have to focus on LeBron and/or Embiid, the driving lanes and midrange tend to be more clogged and there are fewer dimes coming out of the frontcourt. This has the biggest negative impact on the two starting wings.

On the other hand, when Brown sits, it seems to unleash Edgecombe alongside LeBron while negatively impacting the scoring volume and efficiency of Embiid and Maxey. LeBron and Edgecombe have the most overlapping playing style with Brown, so perhaps his absence lets them play more to their natural tendencies. Meanwhile, Brown is the best wing scorer and off-ball threat on the 76ers, so his absence might allow opponents to focus their defensive energy more on the two primary options in Embiid and Maxey.

Fantasy and betting strategy
The biggest area of applicability for this data is in preparing for back-to-backs. Both Embiid and LeBron are routinely sitting one-half of every back-to-back that the 76ers play, typically not the same one.

If these trends continue throughout the season, fantasy and DFS managers and/or points prop betters might consider if there might be better options than Brown or Edgecombe for both halves of back-to-backs.
Fantasy managers that set their lineups weekly should also note how many back-to-backs and games are in a given week, and consider whether LeBron and/or Embiid might be worth starting in a week where they might play only one or two games due to sitting halves of back-to-backs.
Points prop betters might expect Maxey and whichever of LeBron or Embiid are playing to have a higher likelihood to hit 'overs' in these back-to-back sets.
When any of the perimeter starters sit, LeBron and Edgecombe make good fantasy/DFS and props targets. Brown is the only perimeter starter to sit multiple games, but all told Brown (3), Maxey (1) and Edgecombe (1) have each missed time. And LeBron and Edgecombe have each increased their scoring and efficiency in those games, while Embiid and Maxey have seen their scoring efficiency drop. In the three games that Embiid has played without Brown and/or Maxey, though, his assists have increased ... perhaps making him a sneaky assists-prop over candidate in those scenarios.

Bottom line, the 76ers are a different team when they have their entire starting five available versus when any of them sit. And by recognizing the differences, you can put your fantasy hoops squad, your DFS lineup or your prop bets in better positions to succeed.

stories.headline: Ryan Giggs bumped down list of oldest Champions League scorers
stories.summary: Ivan Perišić became the fourth-oldest Champions League scorer by converting a first-half penalty kick in PSV Eindhoven's 5-1 loss to Real Madrid on Tuesday.
stories.body:
Ivan Perišić became the fourth-oldest Champions League scorer by converting a first-half penalty in PSV Eindhoven's 5-1 loss to Real Madrid on Tuesday.

Perišić scored from the penalty spot in the 32nd minute to give PSV the lead during the league-phase game at the Bernabeu.

At 37 years, 295 days, the Croatian calmly hit the top right corner as Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois dived the other way. The penalty was awarded after video review for a foul by Madrid midfielder Aurélien Tchouaméni on Sven Mijnans.

Perišić moved ahead of Ryan Giggs, who scored at 37 years, 289 days, and Sergio Ramos, who scored at 37 years, 257 days.

Giggs scored his goal against Benfica back in 2011 when playing for Manchester United. After falling behind to an early Oscar Cardozo opener, Giggs became the oldest goalscorer in the Champions League at the time when he restored parity for United with a crisp strike from the edge of the area.

- Real Madrid stay perfect in UCL after Bellingham ignites five-goal second half

- Bellingham credits Mourinho 'full stop' for stellar form after Madrid stunner

stories.headline: Max Verstappen admits to 40-hour GTA VI spree as he won Las Vegas GP
stories.summary: Max Verstappen claims he had already clocked 40 hours of Grand Theft Auto VI before his brilliant Las Vegas Grand Prix win at the weekend.
stories.body:
Max Verstappen claims he had already clocked 40 hours of Grand Theft Auto VI before his brilliant Las Vegas Grand Prix win at the weekend.

Verstappen delivered a masterclass of how to race with F1's new engines to win in Sin City, a race which saw an incredible 35 lead changes, but has since revealed that much of his downtime was spent binging through Rockstar's highly-anticipated new game, which came out on Nov. 19.

Revealing the total gameplay time to teammates on the Twitch channel of his esports team, Verstappen Sim Racing, formerly known as Team Redline, he was then asked if his flight home felt like the quickest ever because of the game.

"No, I was sleeping on the plane," he replied. "I played a lot in the evening and the morning in Vegas."

The release of the game coincided with the start of the on-track schedule in Vegas.

Verstappen was one of the drivers who admitted during media day on Wednesday that he had already pre-downloaded the game ready to play, which came out at midnight leading into Thursday.

The schedule followed with two practice sessions on Nov. 19, then qualifying and the race at 8 p.m. local time on Nov. 20 and 21 respectively.

When one of his fellow Twitch streamers quipped it was time well spent, he added: "Yeah! It's not like I can go out anyway."

Verstappen later revealed he does not watch any of the cut scenes around the game's story.

"I'm over 80% of the missions," he added.

- Lewis Hamilton, Charles Leclerc 'unmanageable' - Ferrari boss

- Lewis Hamilton: I could have beaten Kimi Antonelli if I was Ferrari No. 1

- Haas confirm Rafa Camara will finish 2026 season with the team

The admission will add another layer to what will likely go down as one of the best and most memorable grand prix performances of his storied career, which also included a brutal putdown of Mercedes rival George Russell, who he claimed is "so far below my level" that he was unfazed by criticism the British driver had made earlier in the week.

Verstappen is known for gaming at all hours during F1 weekends.

In 2024, Red Bull's then-racing advisor Helmut Marko had to ask the Dutchman to stop streaming himself playing late-night sim racing sessions with Team Redline in the middle of the night and early hours of the morning during F1 weekends.

Verstappen later said the yo-yo Vegas race was something he had only ever experienced playing Mario Kart before.

stories.summary: The couple met in 2021 and was engaged in 2024 before marrying at their alma mater's Memorial Church.
stories.body:
Cameron Brink and Ben Felter have officially tied the knot after holding a ceremony on Nov. 14 at their alma mater Stanford's Memorial Church.

According to a report Tuesday from Vogue Magazine, which shared behind-the-scenes details and images, the Los Angeles Sparks forward had four bridal looks, including a custom dress from bridal designer Danielle Frankel for the ceremony, and another for the reception.

Golden State Warriors star Stephen Curry and his wife, Ayesha, were among those in attendance. Curry and Brink are godsiblings as their fathers were teammates at Virginia Tech, and their mothers were roommates on campus.

The reception was at Ritz-Carlton, Half Moon Bay, while vows were exchanged at Memorial Church, one of the earliest interdenominational churches in the West. The waiting list to get married there can be up to four years, but alumni receive a shorter period, according to Vogue. The couple told the magazine that they always knew they wanted to wed there.

"Walking past the ornate mosaics on my way to class was always the best part of my day," Brink said.

Brink and Felter met at Stanford in the fall of 2020. The two began dating in March 2021 after Felter sent Brink an email in which he included his phone number. Felter, who rowed at Stanford, proposed to Brink in Paris in September 2024.

The No. 2 pick in the 2024 WNBA draft, Brink averaged a career-high 9.5 points plus five rebounds and 1.8 blocks for Los Angeles in the 2026 season.

stories.headline: Price tag for Tassie's new AFL stadium goes up, again
stories.summary: The estimated cost of a new 23,000-seat waterfront venue, set to eventually become the home of the Tasmania Devils, has risen again.
stories.body:
Tasmania's new AFL stadium has suffered another cost blowout, causing the premier to break a promise to cap the state's spend as critics fear the end price will be far higher.

The cost estimate for the 23,000-seat roofed venue at Macquarie Point in Hobart has increased from $1.13 billion to $1.23 billion.

On top of the figure is $132 million for broader precinct infrastructure, project delivery costs of $183 million and unspecified contingencies, taking the total to $1.54 billion.

Premier Jeremy Rockliff previously pledged to cap Tasmania's contribution to the build at $875 million as part of a deal to get the project through parliament.

But he conceded on Tuesday the state would have to cover the slated $100 million increase via extra borrowings.

"The previous cost estimate, which we announced ... some 14 months ago, there's been a lot of water under the bridge since that point," Mr Rockliff said.

The premier confirmed the project wouldn't head back to parliament for the approval of the necessary extra funding, despite previous assurances it would.

The latest estimate reflects increases in the cost of construction, sustained high oil and materials prices, higher labour costs and its complexity, the state government said.

The stadium is expected to be ready for the 2031 AFL season and was a condition of the Tasmania Devils being granted a licence to enter into the national competition in 2028.

It initially had a price tag of $715 million.

Mr Rockliff said the state had reached out to the federal government and AFL for extra money on top of their $240 million and $15 million contributions.

Anti-stadium group Our Place Hobart said the new cost estimate failed to take into account other factors, including the interest bill and the exact cost of contingencies.

Greens leader Rosalie Woodruff described the ongoing cost increases as a deep betrayal of Tasmanians.

"Who knows where the final price for the stadium will end up?" she said.

"What we do know is there's been now a fifth major cost blowout and there's not yet a contract price locked in for this massive project."

Federal independent MP Andrew Wilkie fears the stadium will end up costing $2 billion.

"Once you add the cost of the debt over a decade, the total cost to the Tasmanian taxpayer is closer to $3.5 billion," he said.

Devils chief executive Brendon Gale said the question of any additional funding from the AFL was a matter for the sport's governing body.

"The politicians can politic. We'll get on with building our club," he said.

"People have their views and are entitled to them. But based on my experience, people never look back. These types of projects transform cities and states."

The release of updated costs came ahead of schedule after the government bowed to political pressure to make the figures public before the end of the parliamentary year.

In mid-October, BESIX Watpac was announced as the preferred builder. A final contract is set to be signed by the end of 2026.

BESIX Watpac recently built a 30,000-seat roofed stadium in Christchurch in New Zealand which cost about $540 million.

Mr Rockliff said the final contract price for the Hobart stadium was unlikely to differ from the $1.23 billion estimate.

The stadium has been deeply divisive in Tasmania amid rising state debt, a stretched health system and other under-pressure services.

The AFL and federal government have been contacted for comment.

stories.headline: 'Can't judge them': who Papenhuyzen wants at the Storm
stories.summary: Ex-Melbourne star Ryan Papenhuyzen has made some big calls on who should be the next Storm coach and the one to keep from Cameron Munster and Harry Grant.
stories.body:
Ryan Papenhuyzen empathises with Cameron Munster but believes Melbourne must prioritise keeping Harry Grant if the NRL powerhouse can't hold on to both superstars.

Munster on Tuesday rejected an offer from the Storm believed to be for one year with the option of another season, labelling the terms "disappointing".

The Storm are also fighting to keep Grant, and Papenhuyzen was unequivocal when asked on Wednesday who the club should target if salary-cap pressures meant only one of the newly crowned Australian World Cup winners could stay.

"I went through something similar as Munster where I thought the club had low-balled me," the happily retired 2020 premiership-winning hero told AAP.

"But having my time out of the game now, they've got their reasons for offering those certain amounts and it might not be enough (for Munster).

"Penrith have done it for years and years. They get to a point where they can't hold their players and they've got a price for their players.

"So I understand Munster's perspective. He wants to earn as much as he can in his career and he wants to win a premiership, so that probably limits his opportunities.

"If a club's got money and they're in a premiership window, it's probably a good chance he'll go to that club."

At 28, skipper Grant is four years younger than Munster and more important long-term to the Storm, Papenhuyzen believes.

"Harry's done a brilliant job in terms of leadership," the ex-Clive Churchill Medallist turned caddy said after playing in the Australian PGA Championship pro-am in Sydney.

"The amount of care he has for everyone in that group and the way he thinks about the game, I feel really sorry for him over the last 12 months (when Melbourne missed the finals) because he's always trying to find new ideas to bring everyone.

"He's a great leader for that club going forward. I'd hate to see him go because he's a player you want to build a club around and I guess Munster is towards the back end of his career.

"He had a great World Cup, but World Cups are different to NRL seasons. You've got to lock in for a month with that, and an NRL season's a long time."

Pressed on who he'd keep as a priority, Papenhuyzen said: "Harry's probably the one leadership-wise. Just his qualities are really admirable.

"You know what Munster brings to the game. He gives you confidence standing next to him, knowing what he's going do, but I just think Harry ..."

With coach Craig Bellamy confirming he is moving on at the end of 2027, Papenhuyzen also suspects Grant might be a better for the Storm's new mentor, whomever that may be.

"Harry's really respected and in terms of trying to keep the culture, he's very open-minded too," the BMW golf correspondent said.

"He's open to new ideas, whereas Munster is very much like Bellamy - he's sort of got his way and it's worked for him for so long.

"Whatever they both decide to do, you can't judge them. It's never a right or wrong decision."

Papenhuyzen believes it would be "awesome" if Billy Slater succeeded Bellamy, but suspects "life is too good" for the Storm legend to be a head NRL coach.

"I love Jyles. If he went back there, I'd be awfully encouraged of how well they're going to go. They'd probably be my two."

But Papenhuyzen, also open to helping out the new coach, nominated Bellamy's son Aaron as a left-field option.

"Aaron's awesome with people," he said.

"He's awesome with the wider playing group and he understands that Craig sometimes pushes the boundaries. Aaron's a bit more like Wendy - Craig's, Craig's wife.

"They're both a bit more more gentle, so you've got that loving, nurturing side and potentially (he could do the job).

"I do know you just need people around you. We'd be silly to say the coach controls everything."

stories.headline: Ripple effects of Tarik Skubal signing on Mets, Dodgers and more
stories.summary: The impact of the record deal for MLB's top free agent extends past his new team to the top suitors who missed out on him.
stories.body:
After finishing 20 games behind the Atlanta Braves and 14 games behind the Philadelphia Phillies in the National League East in 2026, locking up the winter's No. 1 free agent, Tarik Skubal, seemingly pushes the New York Mets closer to the teams that have largely dominated their division this decade.

That will be the case in 2027, anyway. The new collective bargaining agreement rules, whatever they are, might not go into effect until 2028 and beyond -- and the Mets' long-term chances for contention could be at risk in the on-going CBA negotiations.

The ripple effects from owner Steve Cohen's $450 million investment in the two-time Cy Young Award winner will not fully take shape until after the labor agreement is concluded. Sources on the management side report that the owners fully expect to come out of the CBA fight with a salary cap -- and will pursue a hard cap on team spending. Of course, the players will have something to say about that; the MLB Players Association leaders say they'll never agree to a cap.

If MLB's economic system changes significantly, how a contract like Skubal's might fit into the owners' vision is unknown. The talk among some rival team officials, in the first hours after the agreement, is how much the Mets have at stake in these CBA negotiations -- especially if the resulting rules don't allow owners to simply buy their way out of salary restrictions with luxury taxes. A hard cap would strangle them.

Francisco Lindor's contract runs through 2031 at an average of $34.1 million per season, and Juan Soto's deal is for $51 million annually through 2039. Bo Bichette is set to make $42 million in 2028. With Skubal added to the books, the Mets will have obligations of $177 million to four players in 2028 and $135 million in 2029-2031. That could account for more than half of their allowed payroll under the owners' proposed system -- and fielding a competitive team would be a challenge, with some players simply inaccessible to the Mets via trade or free agency because of the attached cost.

Cohen is the wealthiest owner in baseball -- though will be second to new Los Angeles Angels owner Stan Kroenke when the sale is officially approved in January -- and if MLB's next financial system includes a hard cap, that financial advantage would be significantly mitigated. The irony would be cruel for Mets' fans: When Cohen purchased the team, the club's followers rejoiced, believing that he would outspend just about everyone in his pursuit of championships -- and he has demonstrated a willingness so far.

But that advantage might well disappear. Cohen made his billions in money management, and this signing seems to be based on a bet that he'll be able to freely maneuver within MLB's financial system -- a bet that other teams aren't willing to make.

Here are some of the other ripples felt throughout the industry in the aftermath of Skubal's record nine-year, $450 million deal, continuing with the impact of his signing on his new team.

New York Mets

David Stearns: In the past, the Mets' head of baseball operations had seemingly been reluctant to invest big dollars in an ace, but Cohen paid for the ace his team needed for its rotation -- and whenever the 2027 season starts, the hope among Mets fans will be restored. That's a good thing.

But the signing of Skubal also ramps up the pressure on Stearns to get the rest of the roster right, which is complicated. The Mets don't really know exactly what they have at second or third base -- the same could have been said for first, but they signed Paul Goldschmidt the day after Skubal -- and their bullpen is a bit of a mess. Cohen offered a vote of confidence for Stearns during the 2026 season, and if the Mets win in 2027, then a lot of the speculation about Stearns' future will evaporate. If they lose after investing in Skubal, the chorus for change will get even louder. That's life in the big city.

Nolan McLean: He has all the stuff and makings of an ace, but now he can share the burden with Skubal -- important in the high-intensity market of New York. McLean won't take the field with Skubal, but he might benefit from Skubal's presence as much as, or more than, anyone else. Not to mention, he and Skubal are similar in their personalities and mindsets.

Los Angeles Dodgers
Owner Mark Walter has said that it's business as usual for the sport's highest-spending team. But Skubal was the first big test of the team's spending powers since Walter started drawing scrutiny from federal investigators, and Skubal is headed to the Mets without receiving a formal offer from the Dodgers -- despite the fact that some friends of Skubal believe his general preference was to return to L.A., if the Dodgers' bid had been equal.

The best and most expensive free agents are coming off the board, and the sense of rival officials is that the Dodgers are more inclined to lean into their robust farm system and to wait for clarity that'll come with the next CBA. The day that the defending champion Dodgers traded for Skubal, they were 10 games over .500, and the starting pitchers that put them in that position -- Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Justin Wrobleski, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow and Shohei Ohtani -- will be back next season, albeit with some questions about how much Ohtani will pitch. Los Angeles will still field an excellent rotation.

Maybe the Dodgers passed on the bidding because of the team's financial situation. Maybe it was because of the uncertainty of what the rules will be in the next CBA. Maybe they didn't want to commit such huge dollars to a player who just turned 30.

Whatever the reason: When was the last time the Dodgers missed out on a player they really, really wanted, and had to have? Before Mookie Betts, right?

San Diego Padres

San Diego's new owners, Jose E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones, sported that new-owner enthusiasm during the playoffs, celebrating the team's successes with the players and pledging that they would continue to spend aggressively. But even the most reckless owners would have to blanche at the risk that the Padres would take on if they spent big this winter, due to the possibility of a future salary cap and the heavy long-term deals on their books. The MLB owners' latest proposal is for a salary cap of $258 million, and the Padres' contractual obligations to Manny Machado, Fernando Tatis Jr. and Xander Bogaerts look like this:

2028: $135 million

2029 $124.7 million

2030 $134.7 million

2031 $122.4 million

2032 $122.4 million

2033 $122.4 million

The Padres could gamble that the CBA talks will conclude with something close to the status quo and sign some needed high-end starters, or the new owners could forge ahead. But adding expensive pitchers would have the potential of boxing in their ability to build rosters into the future.

Toronto Blue Jays

The pairing of Skubal and Dylan Cease, in front of Trey Yesavage, would've given Toronto a daunting rotation, and it appears the Jays finished second to the Mets in the bidding for Skubal.

But the Blue Jays have 13 years and about $460 million remaining in their obligation to Vladimir Guerrero Jr. and another $30 million a year over the next six years to Cease. Adding Skubal's monster contract would have potentially created a very top-heavy payroll situation.

Their pursuit of Skubal now, however, tells you how serious the Jays are about upgrading right now, and they could turn their attention to Freddy Peralta and/or one of the best players in the position player group, like Brandon Lowe. "They've got money burning a hole in their pocket and they're going to do something," one official said.

Detroit Tigers

After Detroit traded Skubal to the Dodgers before this past trade deadline, a rival executive lauded the package of young players the Tigers received in return -- then paused and added, "The Tigers don't look the same without him, do they?"

There was some speculation that maybe Detroit would play 3-D chess and sign Skubal after getting the package of prospects for him, but in the end, the cost to sign Skubal on a long-term deal was always going to be beyond where the Tigers carry their payroll. So what do they have now?

The rotation of Framber Valdez, Troy Melton (who just signed a long-term deal), Keider Montero and Jackson Jobe could be good. The everyday lineup led by Kevin McGonigle has some promise. Detroit will compete in the increasingly competitive AL Central.

But over the past three years Skubal pitched for them, they were arguably the majors' best team on the days he took the mound. He will be missed.

stories.headline: How upsets in the 2026 NFL season have upended survivor pools
stories.summary: Why spend up to nearly $80,000 in order to win a survivor contest over halfway through the NFL season?
stories.body:
Paul Jager was browsing the marketplace for Splash Sports' Survivor World Championship on Friday, Nov. 20, when one specific entry caught his eye ahead of Week 11. The seller had other entries listed and hadn't yet listed this one, but Jager found it and was in awe at the teams used to get it to this point. He knew he had to have it.

Jager purchased the entry on the marketplace for $133,000, the largest transaction that Splash has facilitated since it launched its flagship contest this season. Upon taking ownership of it, he made his Week 11 pick: the Pittsburgh Steelers to defeat the Philadelphia Eagles.

"If I can get through with the Steelers, this entry is set up to win the whole thing," Jager told ESPN of his mindset at the time. "I was like, 'I'm going to take one chance, and if Pittsburgh wins, I am literally set.' I knew five minutes into the game, I was regretting taking Pittsburgh."

The Steelers lost to their in-state rivals, ending that entry's hopes of winning at least a share of the $21 million grand prize. But Jager wasn't out of the running. The investor by trade in Kansas City, Kansas who dabbles a lot in sports betting, currently has six entries alive at Splash and two in Circa Sports' famed Survivor contest, which features a prize pool of over $25 million this season.

Jager's experience is part of what's shaping up to be the new normal for players in high-stakes survivor contests. It fits perfectly into the new look for a sports betting world that is increasingly taking a more stock market-esque approach.

When Splash announced its completely online contest before this season, it was with the goal of expanding the space on top of the remarkable bedrock Circa (which requires in-person registration and proxies) has built since 2020. That included a built-in marketplace that allows players to buy and sell whole or partial tickets within the app using their connected payment methods. So far this season, Splash has already facilitated more than $4 million in transactions.

Circa also launched its own official marketplace by partnering with online platform Survivor Sweat. Circa Sports director of operations Jeff Benson says that the partnership "has driven significantly more engagement and activity than in previous years."

Gabe Patgorski, a former Circa champion, current contestant and founder of the research website Survivor Atlas, describes the contest as more "portfolio-style," given that there is no limit to the number of entries each player can have. Contestants can be more liberal with their selections, knowing that the quantity of entries they keep alive will just increase each's value, if nothing else.

It's a whole new branch of strategy in a game with over 21 sextillion possible combinations throughout the season. And when the stakes are as high as $1,000 per entry, players are looking for any edge they can get to ultimately come out profitable.

"The marketplace is a really cool way to turn any static entry you have in a contest to a tradable asset that you can get out of, or take some chips off the table at any time in the year, or buy back in. And so we've actually seen way more activity than I would've expected," Splash co-founder and co-CEO TJ Ross told ESPN.

Some of the trade activity comes after a particularly brutal first seven weeks of the season whittled down the fields to a fraction of the original entries. Over that span, favorites of seven points or greater -- the teams toward which many survivor contestants gravitate -- lost eight games straight-up, marking the first time since 1972 in which each of the first seven weeks of the season featured such an upset, according to ESPN Research.

Those results had an extensive impact on survivor contests: Following Week 7, Circa Survivor had lost 97.4% of its field (24,357 of the 25,017 entries). Entering Week 12, Circa Grandissimo, the $100,000 entry contest with a $7.7 million prize pool, is down to just three players from the 77 who started.

"In short, 2026 has combined the largest field Circa has ever seen with a run of upsets concentrated on the most popular survivor selections," Benson told ESPN via email after Week 7. "The absolute carnage is record-setting in scale; the underlying dynamic (chalk getting eliminated in bunches) is a familiar and defining feature of the format, just playing out more dramatically this year."

Though the raw volume of eliminations seems shocking, the early portion of the 2026 season was actually not the most carnage the contest has experienced by percentage. That honor belongs to the infamous 2024 season, which saw 99.5% of the field eliminated going into Week 8. The 2022 campaign had 98.0% of its field gone by the same time, which ultimately produced only two winners that year, the fewest in the contest's history.

The favorites have been more reliable since Week 7; the top four most-picked teams in Circa Survivor have won each week and favorites of at least seven points have gone 16-1 straight up from Week 8 through Sunday's games. Week 11 featured an average point spread of 8, the third-largest for any week (excluding the final two weeks of the season in which playoff positioning can dramatically affect spreads) in the last 50 years, per ESPN Research.

Players in the high-stakes contests must now brace for the holiday season. In the Circa pool, each entry must choose a team playing in one of the five Thanksgiving-adjacent games and one of the four Christmas-adjacent games, in addition to the usual games on Sunday and Monday. In Splash, each entry must choose two teams in Weeks 12 through 16, as well as in Week 9, regardless of when they are played.

"It's felt like a normal survivor season to me so far, very different from last year but similar to 2024 and 2022 in terms of pace of eliminations," 2025 Circa Survivor champion Jason Somerville told ESPN over text. He has one entry still alive in Circa. "It never feels real to me 'til Thanksgiving anyway, so fingers crossed I have some decisions to make in December."

The way this season has played out supports the notion that this could be a much more generous holiday season for the contestants than usual, especially with how things shook out at the NFL trade deadline.

Patgorski noticed that many of the already bad teams got worse at this season's deadline, and teams that began the season with high hopes -- like the Indianapolis Colts and Philadelphia Eagles -- became big sellers. There are also teams dealing with injured or underperforming quarterbacks, like the Baltimore Ravens, Los Angeles Chargers and New England Patriots, for whom the bottom has fallen out.

"The path to the end seems a lot easier for almost everyone," said Patgorski. "Every week there are so many big favorites where people are going, 'Oh, that's a lock. That's a free square.' And it's a pretty big shift from a few weeks ago where people thought, 'Okay, this contest has a big chance not to go to the end.' And now, everyone's thinking, 'Oh, there's going to be 50 winners. It's so easy to get to Christmas now. It's so easy to get to the end.'"

Philadelphia presents a juicy opportunity for Circa players given it is one of the few teams playing in both the Thanksgiving and Christmas mini-weeks ... but that in itself creates a paradoxical dilemma unique to high-end survivor contests.

As of Tuesday, the Eagles are 8.5-point road underdogs to the Dallas Cowboys on Thanksgiving according to DraftKings, easily the largest spread between the five games that make up the Wednesday-through-Friday slate. Patgorski estimates that 60-70% of the field will pick Dallas.

"The math says you're supposed to avoid that just because randomness happens often enough to pop that bubble. I think a lot of players have a sense of that, but of course you have to weigh that against, 'Well, maybe it's worth joining the crowd because my entry is strong enough where I'm fine just getting through Thanksgiving,'" he said. "That's kind of the most exciting survivor thing of the year, is the big Thanksgiving bottleneck."

One of the nuances of both competitions is that with each passing week and the continuing eliminations of teams, the implied value of each remaining entry increases in line with the theoretical share of the winners' pot. In Circa, the current average value of each entry has grown to $47,742 while Splash entries are valued at $81,395, according to Survivor Atlas. This in turn creates a market for differentiated entries, with contestants able to buy or sell shares or entire entries to lock in profits, mitigate risk and increase their chances at a share of the pot.

This is when players like Jager, banking on the marketplace to deliver them a deal, spring into action. While the $133,000 entry purchase didn't ultimately work out, he's confident in the rest of the season and is open to selling partial or full entries if he can make it through the contests' Thanksgiving double pick weeks to ensure some profit.

"I just feel really strongly about my path. I took some chances earlier in the year and used some teams like the Jets, Cleveland, Carolina, the Raiders. Some teams that you might not feel comfortable picking in the future," he said. "So it makes those entries a lot more valuable because I have a lot of good teams left to use. And then obviously the more valuable it is, the more I can sell pieces of that for.

"But as Mike Tyson said, 'Everybody has a plan until you get punched in the mouth.'"

stories.headline: Cooper Flagg has 24 points and 12 assists as Mavericks beat Nuggets 120-101 in NBA Cup contest
stories.summary: — Cooper Flagg scored 24 points and tied a career-high with 12 assists as the Dallas Mavericks beat the Denver Nuggets 120-101 on Tuesday night, moving into the driver's seat to win their NBA Cup group.
stories.body:
DENVER -- — Cooper Flagg scored 24 points and tied a career-high with 12 assists as the Dallas Mavericks beat the Denver Nuggets 120-101 on Tuesday night, moving into the driver's seat to win their NBA Cup group.


The Mavericks can clinch a spot in the knockout round as soon as Wednesday if Phoenix loses at Houston. The stakes were high entering this game with both Dallas and Denver 2-0 in West Group A play. The Nuggets have never advanced out of the group stage in the NBA Cup. They're still in the running for a wild card.


Reserve P.J. Washington Jr. had 14 points after missing the last two games with an illness. The Mavericks dominated Denver in points in the paint, 68-38, and fast-break points, 35-7, in extending their winning streak to four games.


It was the 11th 20-point double-double for Flagg, tying him with Dwight Howard for the second-most by a teen in NBA history. LeBron James leads the list with 18. Flagg doesn’t turn 20 until Dec. 21.


Nikola Jokic, the Western Conference player of the week, finished with 18 points, 11 rebounds and five assists. Jamal Murray added 20 as Denver's three-game win streak was halted.


Trailing by 19 at halftime, the Nuggets whittled the deficit to 80-77 with 1:11 left in the third. The Mavericks quickly built it back up.


The Mavericks were cold out of gate on Denver's red NBA Cup-themed floor, going 0 for 6 before hitting three straight 3-pointers. From there, they took off.


Dallas ended the first half on a 15-0 run to take a 58-39 lead as the Nuggets walked off the court to a smattering of boos.


Up next
Mavericks: At Phoenix on Friday to finish group play.


Nuggets: At Utah on Friday to wrap up group play.

stories.headline: Vinícius Júnior praised by Jude Bellingham: Critics want 'excuse to hammer him'
stories.summary: Jude Bellingham backed Vinícius Júnior to silence his critics after the winger shone in Real Madrid's 5-1 Champions League win over PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday.
stories.body:
Jude Bellingham backed Vinícius Júnior to silence his critics after the winger shone in Real Madrid's 5-1 Champions League win over PSV Eindhoven on Tuesday.

Brazil international Vinícius has had a tough season -- losing his place in the Madrid team to new signing Yan Diomande and being hit with a four-game ban after being sent off last month -- but impressed after being handed a start against PSV.

Vinícius signed a new long-term deal at the Bernabéu last summer having been linked with a move away, and admitted during the international break that speculation over his future, coupled with the World Cup, had affected his pre-season preparations.

"I thought [Vinícius] had a brilliant game," Bellingham told TNT Sports. "In the first half, everyone was one or two steps off, but in the second half I thought the level of everyone improved massively, and he was fantastic.

"It looked like it was going to be one of those games where he didn't quite get his goal, and I know for him, that kind of stuff will weigh on him at the moment. I think everyone is out to get him a little bit. Everyone wants an excuse to just hammer him.

"I think it was the best moment of the game for us as a club, as a team and for him that he could get that goal, it matched his performance in the second half."

Bernardo Silva on Vinícius Júnior: 'We see him smiling'

Vinícius' 87th-minute strike -- set up by Bellingham -- was his first Champions League goal this season, while he's also only found the net once in LaLiga.

"For the team it's good that he's with a happy face, we see him smiling," midfielder Bernardo Silva told TNT Sports. "He's coming very strong to this part of the season, and we definitely need him. If you want to win big things you have to count on these types of players."

- Jobe Bellingham teases Jude over wonder-goal: 'Off his shin!'

- Bellingham credits Mourinho 'full stop' for stellar form after Madrid stunner

- Champions League recap: Arsenal drop points vs. Dortmund, Madrid go top

Bellingham was outstanding against PSV, with coach José Mourinho calling him "the best midfielder in the world."

"[Bellingham] is very special," Silva said. "He's a player who can create something very different at any moment. He was a big part of the way we played in the second half.

"Physically he's very strong, he allows us to get to the second ball and then attack. He's good at everything."

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: What to watch in Wednesday's massive 14-game schedule
stories.summary: Find game previews, betting intel, broadcast information, stats and highlights here.
stories.body:
A special week continues for hockey fans. With no games Thursday, there will be 14 games Wednesday, 15 on Friday and 13 on Saturday.

And our usual reminder: Since 2005-06, around 77% of the teams in playoff position as of American Thanksgiving have maintained that spot at the season's end.

What's on tap in those 14 games tonight? Read on for a look at what you need to know for the game, including betting info and broadcast details.

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Winnipeg Jets at Boston Bruins

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | BOS -155, O/U: 6.5

The Jets have been one of the NHL's pleasant surprises this season, particularly since trading Connor Hellebuyck to the Devils.

The winning didn't start right away, but in the past 10 games, they have gone 8-1-1, and are right in the mix for the Western wild cards; they enter Wednesday a tiebreaker behind the Blues for the second spot.

The Bruins had higher expectations this season after making the 2026 playoffs, and although they've fallen from their prior perch of tops in the Atlantic Division, they hold the first Eastern wild card.

This is the second and final game of the season series between the clubs, after the Bruins won 4-3 in overtime in Winnipeg back on Oct. 2.

Keep an eye on Winnipeg's Kyle Connor (32 points) and Boston's David Pastrnak (31), who lead their respective teams in scoring.

New York Rangers at Buffalo Sabres

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | BUF -135, O/U: 6.5

After Buffalo's playoff drought ended this past spring, it looked like a little wind had been taken out of the Sabres' sails. Does a 6-2 win over the Lightning on Sunday get them rolling again?

On the other side, the Rangers missed the 2026 playoffs and an early injury to Igor Shesterkin made it seem like they'd miss the '27 edition too. They've played well in front of Dylan Garand and Joonas Korpisalo, however, and enter this game in third place in the Metro.

This is the first game between the clubs in 2026-27 after the Sabres took two out of three against the Rangers in 2025-26. U.S. Olympian Tage Thompson tops the Sabres' scoring leaderboard (17 goals, 11 assists), while U.S. Olympic snub Adam Fox leads the Blueshirts (two goals, 24 assists).

Carolina Hurricanes at Tampa Bay Lightning

7 p.m. ET (TNT) | CAR -130, O/U: 6.5

Does the Eastern Conference run through one of these two teams? The Canes are on top of the conference standings, with 39 points through 24 games, while the Lightning are third, with 32 through 23.

One fun matchup to watch is in goal. Tampa's Andrei Vasilevskiy is one of the greatest netminders of this generation, with his name on the Stanley Cup multiple teams and Vezina Trophy wins under his belt too. He's racked up 11 wins already, but with a 2.59 goals-against average and .895 save percentage.

On the other side, it's his countryman Pyotr Kochetkov, who is having a breakout season at age 27. Kochetkov has a 13-1-1 record, with a 1.80 GAA and .911 SV%.

Up front, there are no surprises; Carolina's Sebastian Aho (13 goals, 20 assists) and Tampa's Nikita Kucherov (10 goals, 22 assists) lead their teams in scoring.

Ottawa Senators at Florida Panthers

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | FLA -130, O/U: 6.5

The first game of the season between these Atlantic contenders was a 5-1 win for the Sens in Ottawa, where the home fans gave Brady Tkachuk a rude welcome back to Canada's capital. How does this one play out?

Ottawa has taken over atop the Atlantic standings heading into Wednesday's action, while Florida is in the second wild-card spot.

A big reason for the Senators' success has been a bounce-back season by goaltender Linus Ullmark. His 1.44 GAA and .941 SV% are both tops in the league, and he looks every bit up to the personal standard he set in his Vezina-winning campaign of 2022-23.

The Panthers haven't gotten that level of goaltending from Jacob Markstrom and Akira Schmid, but their skater group is one of the NHL's most dangerous (in both senses of the term) -- and could get Aleksander Barkov back within the next few games. Does he make his dramatic return Wednesday?

St. Louis Blues at New York Islanders

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NYI -115, O/U: 5.5

A sneaky-good game here, as both teams are right in the wild-card mix in their respective conference.

The Isles begin the day a tiebreaker behind the Rangers for third in the Metro Division, while the Blues hold the second Western wild card.

Each team is also witnessing a breakout this season. For the Isles, it's Matthew Schaefer -- and yes, 26 points through 23 games is a breakout even though he unanimously won the Calder Trophy last season. His current pace of 94 points would be 35 more than his rookie campaign, and would likely earn him some Norris Trophy votes.

For the Blues, it's Joel Hofer, who has taken over command of the Blues' crease. Entering this game he's run up a 10-6-1 record along with a 2.35 GAA and .919% (both ratios are top 10 in the NHL).

Calgary Flames at Pittsburgh Penguins

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | PIT -155, O/U: 6.5

Did anyone out there think the Flames would be ahead of the Penguins in the league-wide standings at the quarter mark?

And yet, here we are. While these two teams might be among the trade deadline sellers down the road, this game could be a fun watch, given that each team is prone to both scoring and allowing bunches of goals depending on the night.

Joel Farabee leads the charge for Calgary with seven goals and 12 assists, while Pittsburgh is led by Erik Karlsson (three goals, 16 assists).

Philadelphia Flyers at Washington Capitals

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | WSH -162, O/U: 6.5

Due to a weird quirk of the NHL schedule, this is Game No. 22 for the Capitals while the Flyers have already played 26; in other words, it's a little misleading that the Flyers are four points ahead in the standings.

Then again, the Caps have lost five straight games heading into this one, so maybe it's not all that misleading.

Washington won the first showdown between these Metro Division rivals back on Oct. 28, with offseason additions Jordan Kyrou and Alex Tuch each scoring two goals. Are they the key for the Capitals to get back on the winning side of things?

New Jersey Devils at Columbus Blue Jackets

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NJ -148, O/U: 6.5

These two squads just played against one another on Monday, in a game whose result (a 3-2 Devils win) was perhaps closer than one might have predicted given their relative position in the standings.

Among current non-injured Devils, Jesper Bratt and Nico Hischier have the most career points against the Blue Jackets (20), while current scoring leader Jack Hughes has 18 points in 15 games.

For Columbus, Sean Monahan is the career leader in points vs. New Jersey (27 in 23 games), although he's day-to-day.

Vancouver Canucks at Detroit Red Wings

7:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | DET -225, O/U: 6.5

To put it charitably, these teams both have an eye on the future. In Detroit's case, that's particularly true after the long-expected Dylan Larkin trade finally came to fruition this week, returning prospect Michael Hage and multiple first-rounders in the swap.

After losing streaks of 10 and seven games this season, the Canucks have had some bouts of impressive play of late; they've gone 3-1-1 in their past five, and those three wins were against the Golden Knights, Mammoth and Wild (all three of them playoff teams this past spring).

The Red Wings haven't been so successful of late, having lost seven of their last eight contests. But perhaps having the Larkin weight off their shoulders will result in some forward momentum here against an opponent that is outmatched -- at least on paper.

Detroit won the first game in the season series, 5-2, back on Oct. 22. That was a Lucas Raymond game, as the Swedish star scored two goals and added an assist.

Nashville Predators at Dallas Stars

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | DAL -185, O/U: 5.5

Game of the Night? This showdown between two current playoff clubs should be a fun one.

Due in part to a five-game winning streak, Dallas has the standings edge as play begins Wednesday, and sits second in the Central. Nashville has slid back a bit from an earlier peak and holds the first Western wild card.

The first matchup went in the Predators' favor; following a goal by Miro Heiskanen 47 seconds in, Juuse Saros was thereafter unsolvable, making 29 saves to secure the 2-1 win. Saros (8-4-4, 2.50 GAA, .916 SV%) and Jake Oettinger (13-4-1, 2.13 GAA, .909 SV%) are both giving their teams a chance to win every night out.

Up front, veteran superstars Filip Forsberg (nine goals, 16 assists) and Mikko Rantanen (10 goals, 18 assists) lead Nashville and Dallas, respectively, in scoring this season.

Utah Mammoth at Minnesota Wild

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | MIN -162, O/U: 6.5

The first meeting of the season between these teams was on Oct. 27, and at that time the two teams were battling for first place in the Central Division. Minnesota won a tightly contested game 3-1.

Things have diverged quite a bit for the teams in the time since.

After winning two of their next three, the Mammoth embarked on a six game winless streak, won their next two, then lost on Monday to the Jets. They are now looking up at six other teams in the Central.

The Wild have earned at least a point in all 12 games since the win over Utah, including eight regulation wins, one W in OT and three losses in extra time.

Will it be more of the same for both clubs here, or another fork in the road?

Montreal Canadiens at Colorado Avalanche

9:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | COL -135, O/U: 6.5

It's Game 2 of the Dylan Larkin Era for the Canadiens, and Game 4 of the Nathan MacKinnon-less Era for the Avalanche.

These two teams played on Nov. 14 in Montreal (the first Avs game without MacKinnon), with the visiting Avs winning 4-1. Do the Habs get their revenge in Denver?

New Canadien Larkin has three goals and 14 assists in 19 career games against the Avalanche, and missed an empty net in his Montreal debut (something MacKinnon knows a little bit about too).

Chicago Blackhawks at Seattle Kraken

9:40 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | SEA -166, O/U: 6.5

The fans in Seattle won't get to see Connor Bedard in this one -- fans anywhere won't get to see him until late March following shoulder surgery -- but the Blackhawks are bringing a rising star to the rink.

Roman Kantserov is a 22-year-old rookie, and he leads Chicago in goals (13) and points (18) this season.

Berkly Catton is not a rookie, but he chose his sophomore season to break out. After finishing with seven goals and 10 assists in 66 games in 2025-26, he already has eight and 10, respectively, through 21 games this season.

The Kraken enter Wednesday a point behind the Sharks for third place in the Pacific Division -- but have played five fewer games.

San Jose Sharks at Anaheim Ducks

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | ANA -155, O/U: 6.5

Speaking of the Sharks, this will be their first game of the season against their in-state rivals, with this showdown taking place in Anaheim. The Ducks begin the game a point behind San Jose (with one game in hand).

For hockey fans who like to watch young superstars, this is the game for you.

Fresh off his absurd 115-point star turn in 2025-26, Macklin Celebrini again leads the Sharks in scoring, with 10 goals and 21 assists so far; he's on pace for "only" 100 points this season.

Anaheim is led by Cutter Gauthier, who has 22 goals and nine assists. Earlier in November, the Arizona native set an NHL record with four hat tricks in a single calendar month -- and he has three games including this one to make it five (or more?)

Reminder: Fans can catch all the action in the NHL streaming hub and on the ESPN App.
